ANIMAL CATEGORIES LESSON · ANIMAL CATEGORIES · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Primates — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the monkey-and-ape family — the family people belong to, one cousin at a time.

What is this?

Primates are the family of monkeys, apes — and people. We all share clever gripping hands, front-facing eyes and big family lives.

What does it mean?

Family is the idea: primates learn from their mothers, play as children, and solve problems with their hands — the same kit you are using to read this card.

What does the child need to know?

Chimpanzees make and use tools — sticks fished into termite mounds; orangutans have arms longer than their legs and rarely touch the ground; baboons live in troops on the savanna; lemurs live only on Madagascar and wave their ringed tails.

Why this matters

Meeting the primates is meeting our own reflection — the first "we are animals too" a child can see with their own eyes.

What it teaches

Fine-motor practice (the primate superpower is the gripping hand), empathy and family-structure talk, and the big science seed: humans are primates.

Words to learn

primateapemonkeychimpanzeeorangutanbaboonlemurtroophandscousins

Say this to your child

“"Primates are our cousins! Clever hands, clever families. The chimpanzee fishes for termites with a stick-tool, the orangutan builds a fresh leaf-nest every night, the baboon lives in a big noisy troop, and the lemur waves its ringed tail!"”

Step by step

  1. Start with the child&rsquo;s own hand: thumb wrapped around a crayon — THAT grip is the primate signature.
  2. The chimpanzee: the toolmaker — it trims a stick, pokes it into a termite mound, and pulls out lunch. It also hugs and holds hands.
  3. The orangutan: the long arm — it swings and climbs, barely touching the ground, and builds a new nest of leaves to sleep in every night.
  4. The baboon: the savanna troop-member — big groups, loud politics, and cheeks it can fill with food like shopping bags.
  5. The lemur: the Madagascan — found wild nowhere else on Earth, and the ringed tail is a flag it carries upright on walks.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the chimpanzee sits with its hands forward, the orangutan hangs by long arms, the baboon shows its long muzzle, and the lemur raises the famous black-and-white rings.

Ask your child

"Are people primates too?" (yes — the same family) "Which primate uses a stick as a tool?" (the chimpanzee) "Where do lemurs live wild?" (only on Madagascar)

What your child can say or do

Your child might fish "termites" (pom-poms) out of a chair-leg "mound" with a stick-tool for a whole afternoon, build a leaf-nest of cushions every night, or walk with an upright tail-scarf, lemur style.

Out in the real world

Zoo ape houses show the hand-grip and the tool use live — the chimpanzee termite-fishing is the card&rsquo;s most repeatable wow. Madagascar is the only lemur country: find it on the map together.

Try it together

Clever-hands minute: stack five blocks, thread three big buttons, turn three pages one at a time, then undo one zipper. Every task is a primate skill — the family superpower is the hand.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is the primate superpower?" (clever gripping hands) "Which primate makes stick-tools?" (the chimpanzee) "Are people primates?" (yes)

This lesson pairs with the Primates flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animal Categories.
